posts.c: Catamount FAQ: everything you've been wondering. How did Catamount start? 🌾 In 1978, Lucy and Jim McCullough opened their historic family farm to skiers, choosing to "farm fun" when the working farm got harder to sustain. In 2019 the McCulloughs, the Trust for Public Land, COFC, the Town, and a small group of dedicated volunteers partnered to protect 393 acres as the Catamount Community Forest for everyone to enjoy. Thank you, Lucy and Jim! 💚 Who runs Catamount? 🏡 The Catamount Community Forest is owned by the Town of Williston. Catamount Outdoor Family Center is the nonprofit that partners with the Town to maintain the trails, run the programs, and host the events. But it's your passes, memberships, and donations that make our work possible. Do I have to pay to use the trails? 💵 Walking, running, and snowshoeing are always complimentary! posts.c: Down a tucked-away alley in Kyoto, and across a small grassy courtyard, sits a modest timber-framed minka, built in the tradition of Japanese vernacular architecture. From the outside, it has a quiet, understated wabi-sabi sensibility. Warm ochre tsuchikabe—traditional earthen plaster walls—meet dark timber framing and kōshi latticework screens, which offer only partial glimpses of what’s within. If the architecture doesn’t give you a hint, the stacks of cork bark and weathered driftwood gathered outside the entrance might.⁣ ⁣ This is @vandaka_plants ’ Kyoto showroom—a rather special destination for those with an appreciation for the unusual. Open just a handful of days each month, it’s a place where plant enthusiasts come in search of Platyceriums: extraordinary epiphytic ferns whose antler-like fronds and sculptural forms seem to blur the boundaries between the botanical and the artistic.⁣ ⁣ Full video is up on ‘Plant One On Me.’ ⁣ ⁣ Link in stories.

Happy Thanksgiving from all of us at BEVS! We are so thankful for our incredible clients, referring veterinary partners, community, and the amazing pets who make what we do so meaningful. Thank you for trusting us to care for your beloved family members, especially during the moments you need us most. As you celebrate today, please remember to keep the holiday treats to the humans! Table scraps can pose serious risks to your pets, including pancreatitis, gastrointestinal upset, and potential toxicity from foods like onions, garlic, grapes, raisins, chocolate, and more. Fatty foods, bones, and other holiday leftovers can also lead to unexpected emergencies. Help keep your furry family members safe, happy, and healthy this Thanksgiving by sticking to their regular diets and keeping tempting foods out of reach. posts.c: A depiction of friends and family gathered around a table laden with enticing dishes, surrounded by harvest bounty: You’d be forgiven, this week, for assuming that such a picture includes Pilgrim hats, turkeys and unfortunate stereotypes. But at the Integrated Arts Academy in Burlington’s Old North End, a new mural by Jozie Furchgott Sourdiffe presents a far more contemporary and inclusive version of that archetypal scene. She modeled the scene’s figures of kids and adults on actual students, parents and staff members. Prayer flags hanging across the front of the dining table in the mural are reproductions of student artworks. The food, animals and plants depicted were all specific suggestions reflecting the many communities and nationalities to which Old North Enders are tied. In the mural, an Asiatic cheetah from Iran shares space with a Somali goat. Vietnamese lotus blossoms under a mangrove tree; boughs bearing maple leaves, pomegranates and olives frame the scene. Hello. My name is Inigo Monturkey. You defrosted my father. Prepare the pie. One of America’s most iconic birds is hard to miss. Unless, of course, it’s flying at you at 50 mph (yes, turkeys can fly short distances) or sprinting toward your kneecaps at 18 mph. Inconceivable? You keep using that word. We don’t think it means what you think it means. But yeah. Lost track of a turkey? Don’t worry. They leave receipts. Male droppings are J-shaped, while female droppings are spiral-shaped. And the larger the diameter, the older the bird. Congratulations. You’re now the weird relative at Thanksgiving who knows how to identify a turkey by its gobble droppings. The kids’ table has been notified. A word of caution: Shiny objects, windows, and bald heads have been known to trigger a turkey’s vengeance mode. Apparently, they take reflections personally. Protect yourself. Also, never go in against a turkey when pie is on the line! NPS Image: A very serious turkey staring through the doors of the J

posts.c: In 2026, our photo editors chose Gabriel Jensen’s (@shallowseasgallery) image of a banded jawfish as our Your Shot Photo of the Year. These fish are known as mouth brooders because they protect their fertilized eggs by holding them in their mouths until they’re ready to hatch. Jensen hovered motionless above over the fish’s burrow in the shallow waters of Florida’s Lake Worth Lagoon for almost an hour to get this shot, using a dim red light to illuminate the fish while trying not to spook it. Discover more about our Nat Geo Your Shot Photo of the Year 2026 at the link in bio.

Is that car floating? 🤔 Your brain can see movement in a completely still image, even when absolutely nothing is moving. Optical illusions exploit the way your brain processes colors, contrast, shadows, and patterns. Some illusions, such as the rotating snakes illusion, can make stationary circles appear to spin because of how your visual system responds to changes in brightness. Surprisingly, your brain doesn’t simply record what your eyes see. It constantly interprets visual information and makes predictions about the world. This explains why two identical lines can appear different lengths, why stationary images seem to move, and why people can perceive the same picture differently. Like this content? With all the wet weather we’ve had recently, it seems like a great moment to look back at some of our most spectacular underwater images! Join us on a trip under the sea: 🦈 Cutting through the darkness, Thomas Peschak’s (@thomaspeschak) photo shows a beam of light from a research boat illuminating the lagoon of Bassas da India. a remote atoll in the Mozambique Channel where young Galapagos sharks live. It’s one of the few places where the Galapagos shark is found beyond the Pacific and is the only known ocean nursery for it, with schools of 50 or more occurring. 🐢 Jordi Chias Pujol (@jordichias), meanwhile, cruised with a green turtle in the shallow water of Armeñime, a small cove off the south coast of Tenerife. The area is a hotspot for green sea turtles, which forage on the plentiful seagrass found there and are used to divers. 🐟 To get this photo, Ellen Cuylaerts (@underwaterellen) was surrounded by schools of glittering silversides swirling around their predators off the coast of

posts.c: An ocean of stars 🌊🌟 These new Hubble images focus on an area of sky toward our Milky Way's galactic bulge, a densely packed, spherical region of stars that surrounds the center of the galaxy’s disk. The observations were part of a survey that will help researchers better interpret upcoming Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope data, as scientists seek to characterize these stars and search for exoplanets in this busy region of our home galaxy. The galactic bulge has been studied by Hubble several times, and these observations add to the mission's continuing legacy of high-precision observations of stars in this region. Once Roman begins science operations, astronomers will gain a greater understanding of this important cosmic site, where almost a quarter of our galaxy's entire stellar mass resides. The first images from Roman will be shared on December 7! Learn more about these views at the link in our bio. Image descriptions: 1 - Blue and white stars fill the field of view. A smattering

posts.c: The earliest known physician in recorded history lived more than 4,600 years ago, long before modern medicine existed. Imhotep, an ancient Egyptian who lived around 2600 BCE, is often credited as one of history’s earliest known physicians. However, evidence of his actual medical practice is limited. He was also an architect and high-ranking official who helped design Egypt’s famous Step Pyramid of Djoser. Surprisingly, Imhotep became so respected that Egyptians eventually worshipped him as a god of medicine and healing. Centuries later, the Greek physician Hippocrates, often called the Father of Medicine, helped establish the idea that diseases had natural causes rather than being punishments from the gods. His name remains associated with the Hippocratic Oath, a symbol of medical ethics today. Like this content? Follow us for more @dadsaysjokes ❤️

Like if you get them 🤣 Onions make you cry because they release a chemical that turns into a mild acid when it touches the moisture in your eyes. When you cut an onion, damaged cells release enzymes that produce a gas called syn-propanethial-S-oxide. This irritates your eyes, triggering tears to wash it away. Surprisingly, chilling onions before cutting them can reduce the amount of irritating gas released. Even more surprisingly, onions have been cultivated for over 5,000 years and were so important in ancient Egypt that they were placed in tombs. Their circular layers symbolized eternity, and archaeologists have found onions associated with Egyptian burial rituals. Onions also contain sulfur compounds that contribute to their distinctive smell and flavor. Like this content? Follow us for more @dadsaysjokes ❤️

Three high voltage pylons stand in the saturated brine of a working salt pond near Newark, on San Francisco Bay, California. The brine is coloured red by microorganisms that thrive in hypersaline water. The darker patterns under the surface are old marsh channels, where the tide once flowed in and out. Around 85% of the bay’s tidal wetlands were lost over the last century and a half, but about 15,000 acres of former salt ponds nearby are now being restored to tidal marsh. What draws me to places like this is that the industrial landscape still carries the outline of the natural one underneath. I photographed it in August 2025, handheld from the open window of a small plane."" - Alex Visbal (@alexvisbal) Alex Visbal won our Wetlands: The Bigger Picture category in #WPY62 for his powerful documentation of how a single engineered line can reshape an entire wetland. This week offers is a time to slow down, reconnect with friends and family, make a few memories, put a bird on it, and maybe spend some time outdoors. Whether it’s a walk in the woods, a visit to a favorite park, or simply enjoying the company of those around you, there’s a lot to be thankful for. Like leftovers. Speaking of food, did you know birds and bison have a mutually beneficial relationship? True story. Birds often hitch ride on a bison in search a good meal. Also, a good taxi in a pinch, though it’s rather stop and go. As bison graze and move through tall grass, they stir up insects that birds can easily catch, while some birds also pick ticks and other parasites from the bison’s hides. It’s a pretty great partnership. Sharing is caring! One animal’s leftovers become another’s feast, and everyone leaves the table (back of a bison) happy. NPS Photos

I used to get confused by the different types of holiday cacti, and honestly, I don’t blame anyone who does. They look pretty similar until you know what to look for... So I decided to draw out the leaf structures (technically stems!) of the three main types to make them easier to tell apart. The Thanksgiving cactus (Schlumbergera truncata) has those distinctive hooked, claw-like edges. It’s actually the one you’ll most commonly find at nurseries, even though it’s often mislabeled as a Christmas cactus. The actual Christmas cactus (Schlumbergera bridgesii) has smaller, smoother edges. Kind of funny that it’s one of the harder ones to find, considering how often we hear the name. Then there’s the Easter cactus (Rhipsalidopsis gaertnerii), which has smoother edges with a little bristly look to them. Of course, you’ll still run into plenty of variations. posts.c: One of the most famous cartoon tropes, characters running off cliffs without falling until they look down, is based on a deliberate violation of physics! Popularized by Looney Tunes, this gag is part of a set of unofficial animation principles often called cartoon physics. Characters can survive explosions, flatten themselves like pancakes, and recover from injuries that would be fatal in real life. Surprisingly, many cartoon tropes originated from practical animation techniques. Characters often wear the same clothes because consistent designs make them easier to animate, while exaggerated facial expressions help communicate emotions instantly. These conventions became so recognizable that audiences understand them without explanation, even when they make absolutely no logical sense. Like this content? Follow us for more @dadsaysjokes ❤️

My favorite Thanksgiving sweet potatoes. When slow-roasted, sweet potatoes get sweeter, louder, and more nuanced than seems possible. The salty, lightly blackened skin provides a heavenly, crispy contrast; you’ll never want them another way. Slow-roasted potatoes rewarm easily at whatever temperature your oven already is. To serve, cut the potatoes into 2-inch slices and arrange cut side-up in a dish. Serve as-is, or with a drizzle of melted salted butter, with or without a little maple syrup, honey, and pepper flakes stirred in. → Slow-Roasted Sweet Potatoes on smittenkitchen.com or linked in profile. → Comment “send recipe” and I’ll DM it to you https://smittenkitchen.com/2018/02/slow-roasted-sweet-potatoes/

posts.c: Raising the bar 🏋️ A brilliant galaxy with a distinctive central bar of stars takes centerstage in this new Hubble view. Called NGC 4394, this galaxy resides about 55 million light-years away. With its graceful spiral arms and bar, NGC 4394 closely resembles what astronomers think our home galaxy, the Milky Way, might look like if we could see it from the outside. Discover more at the link in our bio! Image description: A barred spiral galaxy fills the image. Its core is a compact, white, brightly-glowing circle; the glow of light around the core stretches out into a yellow bar of light that spans across the center of the galaxy’s disk. Beyond the galaxy’s bar, thin, dark, dust filaments follow a broad circle that spins outward into the galaxy’s two spiral arms dotted with blue and pink spots that indicate areas of young stars and star formation. Image credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, E. Peng, D. Thilker and the MAUVE-HST Team #NASA #Hubble #galaxy #universe #space

If you’re looking for a simple seafood recommendation this mahi-ght be the one! Buy: ✅ Mahi mahi caught by U.S. fisheries Avoid: 🛑 Imported mahi mahi Mahi are large pelagic fish that mature quickly and have lots of offspring! That makes them less susceptible to overfishing. The main environmental sustainability concerns come from how they’re caught. Fishers use longlines and purse seines to capture these flashy fish, but these methods can have a lot of bycatch if not properly managed. Sticking with U.S.-caught mahi is a good way to ensure your fish comes from strictly regulated fisheries that take measures to reduce bycatch. 🐬Dolphinitely a better choice for the sea! #SeafoodWatch #SustainableSeafood #MahiMahi #Dolphinfish #USCaughtSeafood

"The Rock Point Center has done so much incredible work to make the natural world accessible for people of all ages and abilities in Burlington. Participants from the Heineberg Community Senior Center visited Rock Point in April to see spring ephemeral plants and flowers. Our participants seldom get to step into the natural world anymore. The staff at the Rock Point Center have done the unsung work of creating a natural space that welcomes in anyone, regardless of age, ability, or wealth. posts.c: Japan has been on our bucket list for a long time.⁣ ⁣ It’s a place where ancient traditions and contemporary creativity seem to coexist in remarkable harmony. Where a deep reverence for nature, shaped in part by Shinto beliefs, finds expression in its architecture, gardens, food, craftsmanship, and everyday life.⁣ ⁣ There’s also a deep enthusiasm for plants and design here that feels almost unparalleled. Where American design sensibilities often gravitate toward the bold, the dramatic, and sometimes the excessive, the Japanese approach seems to favor restraint, subtlety, and a more contemplative relationship with space and nature.⁣ ⁣ This November, we finally made it out to Japan.⁣ ⁣ Traveling halfway around the world for our Group Botanical Tour, we spent time exploring Kyoto, Osaka, Kobe, and Nara — and came away with so much inspiration — from both the sculptural landscapes and exquisite architecture to the mundane, everyday aspects of living.⁣ ⁣ From tucked-away plant shops and ext
posts.cp: Japan has been on our bucket list for a long time

It tells the story of the political, economic, social, cultural, and demographic changes that transformed America as industrialization reshaped the nation in the years following the Civil War. Established in 1940, Vanderbilt Mansion National Historic Site preserves the fully furnished, 54-room mansion in Hyde Park, New York. Built between 1896 and 1899 for Frederick William Vanderbilt and his wife, Louise, the mansion sits amid a spectacular landscape overlooking the Hudson River and the distant Catskill Mountains. The estate offers a glimpse into the world of Gilded Age wealth, lavish entertaining, and rigid social hierarchies. For America’s newly wealthy, having the fortune, the mansion, and th

Would you cut your own Christmas tree in the Green Mountain National Forest? For just $5? It’s one of our favorite holiday traditions! For just $5 per tree (plus a $2.50 online service fee on recreation.gov), you can get a permit, head into the woods, and bring home your very own wild Christmas tree. We’ve been doing this for 20 years, and every year is a little different. Sometimes we find a beauty. Sometimes we bring home a Charlie Brown tree. But it’s always so much fun! A few things to know before you go: 🌲 Permits are $5 per tree, with a limit of two per household. 🌲 Trees must be 20 feet tall or less. 🌲 You can only cut in designated areas of the National Forest. 🌲 Bring a saw, rope, a tarp (or sled), and a little patience. 🌲 Bringing your pups is part of the fun. You can purchase your permit online through Recreation.gov. Be sure to download the harvest map and check the rules before heading out. Share this with someone who needs a little winter magic, and be sure to follow @ver

So many cosmic questions await. More answers will come with the start of the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope's science operations. But Hubble's mission continues, since both observatories were designed to seek knowledge on different types of astronomical questions. For example, Roman’s design is optimized to examine things like our universe’s large-scale structure, the interplay of dark matter and dark energy, and the variety and abundance of exoplanets. Hubble is capable of more detailed observations of our solar system, star formation, the intergalactic medium, energetic ultraviolet light events, and exoplanet atmospheres. And the approach of both missions to observations differs, too. While Roman will mostly do large-scale surveys pre-planned by scientists, which will be a treasure trove for years to come, Hubble will do mostly pointed, detailed observations of specific objects and regions as proposed by individual science teams. For a few hours this summer, streets across Vermont were transformed. The streets that normally divide our neighborhoods with fast traffic suddenly became filled with people. When we close our streets to traffic for a block party, people can safely drag their whole lives out onto the road. They play games and music, eat potluck dinners, chat and meet their neighbors, maybe for the very first time. The most painful part of a block party is announcing that it’s over. Kids drag their feet in the middle of their games, adults cut their conversations short, and the cars start flowing through again. What if it didn’t have to end? Read Jack Evan's full report, Streets Should Be Places, at the link in our bio.

posts.c: Onions have layers. Stars have layers. Webb’s mid-infrared instrument is giving us new details on supernova remnant Cas A, helping astronomers chronicle the structure and evolution of Cas A’s original star. Stars form as gravity causes clouds of dust and gas to collapse, ultimately triggering the internal fusing of hydrogen into helium. Mechanisms within the star cause it to fuse heavier and heavier elements and as this process repeats, a star can develop shells of these elements. When high mass stars end their lives dramatically in a supernova explosion, the elements created within the star get spread into space, ultimately allowing new stars to form. Webb (guided by data from the retired Spitzer Space Telescope - slide 2) found evidence that shortly before the supernova explosion, the shells of elements created in the star merge, causing the layers to mix, changing the structure of the star, and thus the chemical composition of its remains. Heading into turkey week, it's a good time to take a moment and reflect on the significance of this singular species. They are unquestionably odd looking, and these days it seems like there are more of them than you can shake a stick at, but don't be fooled. Vermont's ubiquitous turkeys are a sign that conservation is working, and for that all of us can be thankful! In very brief, turkeys are one of our native species whose abundance today reflects generations of dedicated work by conservationists of all stripes. This as recently as the early 1900s, Vermont was turkey-less on account of habitat loss and unregulated hunting In the 1960s, Vermonters decided to do something about that, and the work of bringing back our wild turkeys began. Fish & Wildlife biologists teamed up with colleagues in New York and captured and translocated wild birds from west of the Finger Lakes to the farmland and woodlots around Pawlet, in Rutland County. It’s hunting season, so don’t just wander into the woods! Stay safe!! 🚨✨ Hunting is an important part of Vermont life and it’s a tradition that goes back thousands of years before America’s founding. Vermont was the first state with constitutional language that protects our community's right to hunt. But with hunting comes risks, so let’s talk openly! To be very blunt… hunting season means there are people outside with guns. I’m listening to gunshots in my backwoods as I write this. Hunting is allowed on all state and national land, including state parks, town forests, and anywhere within the Green Mountain National Forest. When you put this together, it’s most of the state that allows hunting. ⭐️ So where is it safe to walk? Fortunately for hikers, there are many nature centers and museums with gun-free trails. Do bears hibernate? Kind of. (That’s a scientific term.) Hear us out. Bears actually enter a state called torpor. Their metabolism slows, their body temperature drops, and they can go for long periods without eating, drinking, or doing much of anything. Essentially, they’ve mastered the art of doing absolutely nothing. It’s a gift. Unlike true hibernators, bears can wake up relatively easily and may even become active during warmer spells. Does that mean they’re leaving the den for happy hour every night? Not quite. But they might stretch their legs, take a little loop around the neighborhood, doom scroll online, or just check whether anything interesting has happened while they’ve been asleep. Flight delays? Email down? And back to the den. NPS Images

Sun sets before 4:30 PM, which means for most of us, the commute home is in the dark. Drivers, WATCH OUT for people biking, walking, and rolling on the street! Before you pass, slow down. Check for oncoming traffic. As you pass, give at least 4 feet of clearance between your passenger mirror and that person biking, walking, or rolling. Slowing down adds seconds to your drive, and lets them get home safely. Bicyclists, CHARGE YOUR LIGHTS! It can be hard to remember when you ride to work or school in the morning light. By law, and for your own safety, you must have a front white light and rear red light to ride on the street. Walkers, rollers, and bicyclists, BE VISIBLE! We know many drivers are distracted in their cars. Do your best to be seen with gear that reflects, wearing lights, and by taking up space and making yourself known. Have you ever wondered how a forest changes over its lifetime? Last week, we introduced you to early-successional forests. As these young forests grow back from a disturbance, they enter their version of the teenaged phase. While they still support some plants and animals, they lack the structural complexity of their younger and more mature counterparts. These forests are no longer young, with abundant and dense trees and shrubs up to 20 ft in height. They also have not reached an older, more mature condition, with multiple layers of vegetation, small gaps in the canopy overhead, large diameter standing dead trees, and large logs on the forest floor. Thoughtful stewardship can help introduce the habitat diversity needed to sustain more biodiverse and resilient forest communities. Get started fostering biodiversity in your forest. “Dark Botanica,” on view through January 23 at Burlington City Arts (@btvcityarts), 135 Church St., #BurlingtonVT, “expands the traditional central themes in still-life painting — love, innocence, sensuality, decay to include the polemical. A flower is never only a flower,” writes Marta Pauer-Tursi (@sohochicnyc) in our current issue. “Upon entering the gallery, Marcie Scudder’s oversize installation, “My Mother’s Garden,” captures the viewer’s imagination. The work drapes across the ceiling and against the street facing glass facade of the gallery as a quilt might drape casually across a bed. Made of hundreds of small hexagonal folded papers and photographs of poppies, thistle, myosotis, and stitched together to create a flow of origami flowers, the work references the artist’s mother who left her a garden when she died,” Pauer-Tursi writes. A bridge of stars 🌟 The galaxy NGC 1672's central bar of stars channels gas towards its core! Located around 49 million light-years away, it belongs to the constellation Dorado. Multiple telescopes come together to showcase the galaxy's cosmic activity. @NASAChandraXray data (purple) highlight growing black holes along the galaxy's central bar and core, merged with @NASAHubble optical light (white, yellow, and blue) and @NASAWebb's infrared observations of dust filaments (red). Image description: At the image's center are two thick, spiraling, dark purple arms that bridge a brilliant white and neon pink core. Those bridging arms create a bar. Longer, wispier arms also spiral out from the core, dotted with gleaming white and pink stars. Image credit: X-ray: NASA/CXC/SAO; Optical: NASA/ESA/STScI/Hubble Heritage Team; Infrared: NASA/ESA/CSA/STScI/J. Lee and T. Williams; Image Processing: NASA/CXC/SAO/L. Frattare, J. Major, K. We want to share an update on Sundzu with all of you who have been holding him in your hearts. Sundzu is continuing to receive around-the-clock treatment for EEHV-HD, and his condition is stabilizing. His wildlife health and care teams are encouraged but remain highly concerned, recognizing that there is still a long road ahead. They remain by his side, bringing all of their expertise to his care. Following the recommendations of the North American EEHV Advisory Group, his treatment has included antiviral medications, fluids, blood and plasma transfusions, and a stem cell infusion. We are extraordinarily grateful for the outpouring of support from around the country, and our teams feel it every day. We’ll share more with you as we’re able, and we appreciate your patience and your compassion as we navigate this together. Thank you for keeping Sundzu, and those caring for him, in your thoughts. *These videos show moments of Sundzu between 2023 and 2025.

Learn more about the long-term planning, negotiations, and local partnerships that have made this reroute possible. GMC crews completed a two-year trail relocation project on Belvidere Mountain. Walk into almost any houseplant shop today, and you’ll likely find enthusiasts gravitating toward big, sculptural Aroids, dramatic foliage, and the bold, waxy blooms of Hoyas. But there’s another group of plants that, while perhaps less showy at first glance, has a history of captivating collectors: the Gesneriads.⁣ ⁣ These plants were once the darlings of the houseplant world. Gloxinias were all the rage in the Victorian era, while African violets, Cape primroses, and lipstick plants enjoyed enormous popularity from the 1950s through the 1980s. So what happened? And why are these plants beginning to find their way back into the spotlight?⁣ ⁣ It might have something to do with their surprisingly diverse personalities. Some have velvety, almost iridescent leaves, dark foliage with contrasting undersides, or intricate silver markings. Cracked drywall? Don’t just tape it and hope. 😬 @tomsilvatoh shows a homeowner the right way to fix a ceiling: 🔨 Find the strapping by drilling a pilot hole from below 🔨 Sandwich the drywall between two screwed-together sheets of plywood 🔨 Prop it tight with a 2x4 and screw it into the strapping 🔨 Mesh tape, compound, texture, done The result? You can’t even see the patch. 👀 Save this for the day your ceiling cracks, and send it to the friend who keeps saying “I’ll fix it eventually.” 😂 . . . . . . . #thisoldhouse #homeimprovements #dıy #homerenovation #drywall

posts.c: This past summer and fall, Vermonters reclaimed their streets as safe, shared spaces through our block party program Streets as Places. For a few hours, instead of traffic, streets were filled with people. Neighbors gathered together to eat, laugh, play, dance, and in many cases, meet for the first time. The streets that normally act as a barrier and separate our homes suddenly became the thing that connects us. Your support during our Year End Appeal helps us to bring more neighbors together. Donate today at the link in our bio. A gift of any size strengthens our programs and advocacy statewide, making it safe, accessible, and fun for everyone to bike, walk, and roll in Vermont.

posts.c: Two stars enter... Webb observed the aftermath of a star merger, helping astronomers piece together the fate of the pair. Stellar mergers are very hard to predict, and thus hard to observe. But in 2023, astronomers noticed an unusual variable star that had a consistent brightness in 2018. By September 2024, the object, nicknamed “Bao,” was starting to brighten and also spew dust. Bao faded in visible light but brightened in infrared in July 2025. When ground-based telescopes caught an eruption on October 17, 2025, multiple telescopes swung into action. Webb’s quick-turn look was cross-referenced with extensive ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared data from telescopes both in space and on the ground, including other NASA missions like NEOWISE, SPHEREx and the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory. I love playing board games! But why are they so annoying to store?! 😩 The boxes are all different sizes which makes them a pain to pull out. Each box is unaesthetic (IMO) with competing loud graphics. So I had a cluttered mess which I then hid away in a closet and my games ended up forgotten instead of played. 🙈 This led me to wonder- what if games didn’t have to stay in their original boxes? Imagine if they looked like a library of beautiful books instead?! What if I could take the board games I already owned and make them over? 📚 I was nervous about trying- I didn’t want to ruin a perfectly good board game. But I decided if it worked, it’d be such an upgrade. I put my idea to the test and started crafting. Spoiler alert- after some trial and error it came together so well! posts.c: There’s no practical reason to grow your own wheat. Buying flour is cheaper in every way… But I grow it anyway. This year I planted out a 3x35' plot. The last time I grew it my yield was pretty mediocre...but I still baked 3-4 sourdough loaves that tasted absolutely amazing Growing the wheat is less than half the job tho - at harvest time you cut it, thresh it (knock the grain loose from the stalks), winnow it (toss it in moving air so the light chaff blows away and the heavy grain falls), and then mill it into flour 3 months of growing + that entire post-processing saga yielded me ~10 pounds of homegrown wheat this summer. More than enough to make a FULLY homegrown banana bread with my own bananas, my own flour, and eggs from the backyard hens Outside of growing my own vanilla and sugarcane, that’s about as close as I’m gonna get to a fully homegrown baked good. Is it practical? Absolutely not. But is it fun? Hell yeah
posts.cp: There’s no practical reason to grow your own wheat

"Just another day working up some feral salmon." If you had to read that twice and are still scratching your head, let us explain! It all has to do with yesterday's post about collecting salmon eggs to raise in our fish hatcheries. Those fish were broodstock who live in the hatchery, but we also work with hatchery-born fish who spend their whole adult lives in the wild, too. Landlocked Atlantic salmon are native to Vermont's bigger lakes, but today very few of these fish successfully reproduce in the wild due to habitat loss that's played out over the past couple hundred years. As we work to improve aquatic habitat quality and connectivity, our hatcheries also raise salmon to release into the wild as smolts. Although these fish are born in the hatchery they can live for many years and grow huge out in the wild, essentially, going feral. posts.c: Rho, Rho, Rho your Oph...🎶 Rho Ophiuchi is a striking star-forming cloud, filled with gas and stars of different sizes and ages. Chandra reveals infant stars that violently flare and produce X-rays. Infrared data from Webb provides views of the cloud’s regions of gas and dust. When this data is made audible, through a process known as data sonification, Chandra’s X-rays become high-pitched glassy tones, along with other sustained sounds to mark the appearance of extended bright sources. The clouds in Webb’s infrared data are mapped as differently pitched sounds, and stars are played as metallic plucks. There is a gap in the middle of the piece due to dark dust clouds that emit very little light. #Space #Universe #Sonification #Astronomy #Stars

🦌...November is when most Vermont outdoorsfolk are thinking about deer, but for our fish culture staff November is also the month of salmon...🐟! Before European colonization, this time of year is when landlocked Atlantic salmon would swim into the tributaries of Vermont’s large lakes to spawn. Now, as we work to keep populations of these prized fish healthy and ultimately to restore them in their native waters, November is the time when we gather salmon eggs to rear in our hatcheries around the state. Pictured here, staff at our Bald Hill Fish Culture Station collect salmon eggs from hatchery-dwelling broodstock to supplement the eggs harvested from feral fish in Vermont's bigger waters of Lake Champlain, Lake Memphremagog, Lake Willoughby and Seymour Lake.

In Vermont, the sugarhouse is a kind of sacred place: a steamy little cabin at the edge of the woods where sap becomes syrup and neighbors gather while the fire burns. It is fitting, then, that the state’s most talked-about new hotel takes its name and its spirit from them. @sugarhousehotelvt has opened in Winooski, a historic mill city just across the river from Burlington, and it is the first hotel the city has ever had. It is also something Marriott has never done anywhere in the world: a hotel designed from the start to run entirely on electricity, produce as much energy as it uses over the course of a year and earn LEED Platinum certification. And yet the first thing you notice isn’t the technology. It’s the timber, the glass and the sense that every corner was made by someone who lives nearby. → Read the full story on 5 Reasons to Visit. #travel #destination #vermont #winooski #newengland

A bighorn sheep's face when someone says, "Nice antlers!" *bighorn sheep sigh* 😑 So, what's the difference between antlers and horns, anyway? Horns are a two-part structure. An interior portion of bone (which is an extension of the skull) is covered by an exterior sheath grown by specialized hair follicles (similar to human fingernails). Horns are usually found on both males and females of pronghorn, bison, and bighorn sheep. Antlers grow as an extension of the animal's skull. They are true bone, a single structure, and generally found only on males of the deer family. Antlers are also shed and re-grown each year, while horns are usually never shed and continue to grow throughout an animal's life. One exception to this rule is the pronghorn, which sheds and re-grows its horn sheath each year. Photo (NPS / Jacob W. Frank): 1. Bighorn sheep ram with large, curved horns. 2. Bull elk with large antlers. 3. Pronghorn buck with horns.

posts.c: Burying food scraps in your garden sounds like an easy way to feed your plants, but there’s a little more soil science involved than you might think. Organic matter doesn’t become plant food overnight. Soil microbes, fungi, and other decomposers have to break it down first, converting complex organic compounds into simpler nutrients that plant roots can eventually absorb. Here’s the catch: decomposition takes time, and fresh organic materials can temporarily tie up nutrients as microbes consume them to do their work. Depending on the material, its carbon-to-nitrogen ratio, and how quickly it breaks down, burying food scraps can actually delay nutrient availability rather than give plants an immediate boost. Materials like raw animal tissue also need time to decompose, which can make nutrient release unpredictable. Asparagus is a perennial because it has an underground storage system that keeps it coming back year after year. The crown, a cluster of buds and roots just below the soil, stores carbohydrates that fuel new spear growth every spring. Its deep, established root system also helps the plant access water and nutrients beyond the reach of many shallow-rooted vegetables. Here’s the interesting part: those feathery ferns aren’t just extra foliage. They’re the plant’s solar panels. Through photosynthesis, they capture sunlight and convert it into sugars, which are transported down to the crown and stored as energy reserves. The more energy the crown accumulates during the growing season, the more resources it has to produce healthy spears in the seasons ahead. That’s why harvesting asparagus too early can set the plant back. Every spear you cut is a potential fern that could have been producing energy for the underground crown. Letting those spears mature allows the plant to build the reserve

Ocean in Motion / La Danza del Mar invites the young and young at heart to connect with ocean life through movement and play. The ocean moves us! Watch as they groom and dive off the rocks. Then, practice your penguin waddle in this new interactive space. A 20-foot-long coral reef includes giant clams and a bluespotted ribbontail ray that glides along the sand. Nearby, clownfish nestle into anemones. Enjoy multiple play areas that are welcoming to visitors of all ages. There’s also plenty of rest areas to relax and check out the ocean views of Monterey Bay! Watch leaping blennies hop across wet stones! Visitors can also follow shapes in the floor to hop from rock to rock like blennies. posts.c: Comment ‘dad’ on this post for an extra dad joke straight to your DM’s 👇 Cars use several types of filters to protect their engines, improve performance, and keep passengers comfortable. Air filters prevent dust and dirt from entering the engine, oil filters remove contaminants from engine oil, and fuel filters stop impurities from reaching the fuel system. These filters help reduce wear, improve efficiency, and extend the lifespan of important components. Cabin air filters also clean the air entering the passenger compartment, trapping dust, pollen, and other airborne particles. Interestingly, a clogged filter can reduce engine performance, restrict airflow, or cause unpleasant smells inside the car, depending on which filter is affected. Regular filter replacement is one of the simplest ways to keep a vehicle running smoothly.

posts.c: We asked this 8-year-old to draw the famous “Cosmic Cliffs” hidden within the Carina Nebula, based on the famous James Webb Space Telescope image. The region is actually the edge of a gigantic, gaseous cavity within NGC 3324, roughly 7,600 light-years away. The cavernous area has been carved from the nebula by the intense ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds from extremely massive, hot, young stars located in the center of the bubble, above the area shown in this image. The high-energy radiation from these stars is sculpting the nebula’s wall by slowly eroding it away. Our artist managed to capture the beauty of this Webb image, along with her version of the telescope itself, a rocket ship, and there is even a cameo of "The Traveler" exploring the cosmos! Credit: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center Producer: Paul Morris Special thanks to Candy Jar, ASMR, and Donut Dan Music Credit: "Pizz with Pizzazz" by Bertrand Allagnat [SACEM] via Illustration Musicale [SACEM], Universal Productio

Best of my time in west mt airy 🩷 the most magical cottagey rowhouse on the most charming street- I put a lot of love into this place to make it feel like home for me- painted the whole dang thing, replaced the light fixtures, planted a whole bunch of plants, and more! I enjoyed her for 2.5 years but it was time for change! I went through a big breakup here- my first and only relationship that lasted 8 years. I lived here alone for a year and a half, becoming a single cat mommy of two, while I healed and found my way back to myself, found new hobbies (tennis, rock climbing, knitting, golfing, following baseball again), prioritizing my friendships and making new ones, learning how to spend comfortable time alone and figure things out for myself after living with someone for so long. I imagine I’ll find my way back to mt airy since I love her so much, but for now I’m back in the city and excited to decorate my new solo (!!!) apt and for all that comes next 💖

My mom passed away 11 years ago of metastatic breast cancer. I went through a double mastectomy, IVF process to freeze eggs, and 18 rounds of carboplatin and taxol chemo. We are so appreciative of all the outpouring of love that we’ve seen from our community and wanted to share an update on what was found after a necropsy was performed on Fiona. The location and anatomy made laparoscopic removal impossible. No treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success, and the necropsy confirmed that no amount of supportive care would have worked. The other hippos, Bibi, Tucker, and Fritz, are eating and behaving normally. It’s difficult to know how they’re feeling, but they appear to be their normal selves. Keepers, vets, staff, and volunteers are shaken and trying to navigate this loss. She meant a lot to a lot of people.
A deal’s a deal. 🍋‍🟩 And Noah made sure we held up our end of it. 🪩 Join us tomorrow night for Afropop Night with The Kwame Vibe @thekwamevibe

It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency. The vet staff tried everything they could to help her after she ingested a hat that ended up in her habitat by accident last week. Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome. The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover. We know everyone in the community will be crushed by this news, as we all are. Please keep her keepers and everyone who tried to help her in your thoughts as they try to navigate and come to terms with this shocking news. They are also, understandably, asking for space at this time.

held.c: As we continue to grieve Nipho alongside you, we’re sharing what we’ve learned about his passing, along with an update on his half-brother, Sundzu. Inhlonipho “Nipho," passed away on Wednesday after a brief battle with one of the most serious diseases facing the world’s elephants, known as EEHV-HD (elephant endotheliotropic herpesvirus hemorrhagic disease). EEHV-HD, which poses no risk to people or other wildlife, is caused by a naturally occurring virus found in Asian and African elephants around the world, both in their native habitats and human care. Most elephants will contract the virus in their lifetime, and many carry it without becoming ill. Younger elephants are particularly vulnerable to complications. Nipho’s illness came on and progressed unusually fast. Our team began treatment right away, even before a definitive diagnosis, and we are continuing to look closely at his case to understand what happened. A new episode of Dad Pod is now available - “Hangin’ with the Burlington Run Club”! In episode #35, Dan Castrigano chats with some of the guys from the Burlington Run Club about their experience running with the group. The short clips featured in the episode were recorded on October 18, October 25, and November 1, 2026. Recording took place outside in various weather conditions, and some of it was recorded while running. Please excuse the background noise—and heavy breathing—in some of the audio. Dad Guild’s Burlington Run Club meets every Sunday morning at the intersection of Staniford Road and the Burlington bike path in Burlington’s New North End neighborhood. From there, the group runs to the walk/bike bridge over the Winooski River and back, for a total of 3.5 miles.
